description:
Per-cert URI fan-out in `Verifier::build_with_aia` (pkix-chain/src/lib.rs:585-681) is bounded only by `AIA_MAX_DEPTH = 5` iterations and by the adapter's own request-level caps; the chain layer itself imposes no cap on `new_uris.len()` per iteration. The loop iterates every cert in the cloned pool (initially `supplied_chain`, growing on each successful fetch), pulls every HTTP(S) URI out of each orphan's AIA extension, dedups against a `HashSet` of previously-tried URIs, then calls `AiaFetcher::batch_fetch(&uri_refs)` on the whole batch.

Attack: caller submits a chain `[attacker_leaf]` whose AIA extension carries 10 000 `caIssuers` URIs. Each is unique (e.g. `http://attacker.example/i.der?n=0001` … `?n=10000`). On iteration 1 the loop emits a `batch_fetch` of 10 000 URIs. The adapter (`pkix-aia-http::HttpFetcher`) issues 10 000 HTTP requests with its 10-second per-request timeout — minutes to hours of wall-clock and network bandwidth for one `verify_one` call.

Going wrong:
- Availability: a single un-validated cert blob drives the chain layer to amplify caller-supplied input by 10000× into the adapter's HTTP transport. Caller-side per-request caps don't help — the multiplier is the chain layer.
- Cost: in cloud / CI environments where outbound HTTP has cost or rate caps, the attacker can exhaust them.
- Resource fairness: a multi-tenant validator (e.g. an MTA's S/MIME validator) can be DoS'd against other tenants' requests.

Mitigation: enforce a `MAX_URIS_PER_CERT` cap (RFC 5280 §4.2.2.1 does not bound the count, but real-world certs have 1-2 caIssuers entries; 8 is generous and 32 is paranoid) inside `aia_extract::ca_issuers_http_uris`, and a `MAX_TOTAL_FETCHES` cap inside `build_with_aia` (e.g. `AIA_MAX_DEPTH * MAX_URIS_PER_CERT`). Surface as a new `Error::AiaFanoutExceeded` or fold into `AiaDepthExceeded` with a documented meaning. Both caps belong as `pub const` so callers can audit and (optionally, see PKIX-q9hv.21) override.

Crypto-security framing: this is an availability / resource-exhaustion class issue, not key-recovery. P1 because it is a live exploitable amplification primitive when a real `AiaFetcher` is wired, not a hypothetical edge case.

Notes:
- Related to PKIX-q9hv.6 (tried_uris dedup is case-sensitive — makes the fan-out even larger because `HTTP://` and `http://` count as distinct).
- Related to PKIX-q9hv.21 (AIA_MAX_DEPTH constant has no Verifier-level override — same shape applies to a hypothetical MAX_URIS_PER_CERT).
- `pkix-aia-http` has a body-size cap on each fetch but no per-fetcher request-count cap; the chain layer is the right place to enforce a per-verification cap.
title: (SEC) AIA fan-out is unbounded per cert — attacker-controlled cert can drive O(N×depth) HTTP fetches
